food.text: Ancient Greek cooking rested on a "Mediterranean triad" of cereals, olives, and grapes, which had many uses and great commercial value. Yet legumes mattered as much or more to the average diet, and research suggests the agricultural system could not have succeeded without growing them.

A typical Greek breakfast was called akratismos and consisted of barley bread dipped in wine, sometimes with figs, dates or olives. Greeks also ate a pancake called tagenias, a word derived from the Greek for "frying pan".
Bread wheat was hard to grow in Mediterranean climates, so white bread made from it was linked to the upper classes. The poor ate coarse brown breads made from emmer wheat and barley.

Until the 8th century BCE the Greek mainland could feed its people, but overpopulation then appeared in many regions. This has been seen as the driving factor behind Greek colonisation, since overseas settlements could house and feed the growing population and send food back to their mother cities.

Athens could not have survived without imported grain from Ukraine. Some Athenian colonies, including the cleruchies of Asia Minor, were important for controlling the wheat supply. Trade in ancient Greece was free, but the state controlled the supply of grain.

Solon, an Athenian lawmaker of the 6th century BCE, prescribed that leavened bread be reserved for feast days. By the end of the 5th century BCE, leavened bread was being sold at the market, though it remained expensive.

The philosopher Pythagoras is considered "the Father of Ethical Vegetarianism". He believed the highest level of spiritual and physical health required a vegetarian diet that excluded meats and other flesh foods.

Bees were kept in ancient Greece to produce honey, which was the only source of sugar known to the ancient Greeks. Husbandry was badly developed because of a lack of available land, and sheep and goats were the most common livestock.

Shipwrecks give evidence of growing trade. Only two were found dating from the 8th century BC, but archaeologists have found forty-six from the 4th century BC. With ships also getting larger, the total volume of trade probably grew by a factor of 30.

When Greece was conquered by Rome in the 2nd century B.C., commercial bakeries became well known and spread. Pliny the Elder suggests bread production moved from the family to the "industrial" thanks to skilled artisans, starting from 171 BCE. Plato had earlier favored home production and described Thearion the baker as an Athenian novelty.

Plato's idea of a healthy diet was balance and moderation of cereals, fruits, vegetables and dairy, with a strong emphasis on moderating meat and wine. He believed that excess food from one source would lead to future ailments.

art.text: Ancient Greek art is famous for its naturalistic but idealized depictions of the human body, in which largely nude male figures were generally the focus of innovation. The rate of stylistic development between about 750 and 300 BC was remarkable by ancient standards, and is best seen in sculpture.
Greek painting has to be largely reconstructed today because of the lack of original survivals of quality. The main exception is the distinct field of painted pottery, which survives in abundance.

Greek architecture is best known for its temples, with the Parthenon regarded, now as in ancient times, as the prime example. Each temple appears to have been conceived as a sculptural entity within the landscape, very often raised on high ground so that the elegance of its proportions and the effects of light on its surfaces could be admired.
The second important surviving type of Greek building was the open-air theatre, with the earliest examples dating from around 525 to 480 BC. Theatres survive all over the Hellenic world.

Some of the best known Hellenistic sculptures are the Winged Victory of Samothrace, the Venus de Milo from the island of Melos, the Dying Gaul, and the group Laocoön and His Sons. They depict Classical themes, but their treatment is far more sensuous and emotional than the austere taste of the Classical period would have allowed.

The particular character of Greek architecture can first be seen in the pottery of the Dorian Greeks from the 10th century BC. It was made with a sense of proportion, symmetry and balance not apparent in similar pottery from Crete and Mycenae, and its decoration was precisely geometric, ordered neatly into zones on each vessel.

Greeks embroidered their clothes with floral and geometric patterns as well as intricate scenes from Greek stories. In Homer's Iliad, Helen is described as wearing a purple textile on which she embroidered a scene of Trojans in battle.

Greek jewelry included rings, wreaths, diadems, bracelets, necklaces and earrings, most commonly in gold and silver. Common designs included plants, animals and figures from Greek mythology, and small gold ornaments were sewn onto clothing so they would glitter as people moved.

After 465 BC, playwrights began using a backdrop or scenic wall called the skené, from which the word scene derives. It hung or stood behind the orchestra and also served as an area where actors could change their costumes. The death of a character was always heard behind the skené, because showing a killing in view of the audience was considered inappropriate, though some scholars argue death was kept off stage mainly for dramatic reasons, not out of prudishness. After 425 BC a stone scene wall called a paraskenia became a common supplement, and by the end of the 5th century BC the skené was two stories high.

By the latter sixth century BC, local elites in Macedonia could acquire exotic Aegean items such as Athenian red figure pottery, fine ceramic perfume flasks, glass, and marble and precious metal ornaments, all of which served as status symbols. By the 5th century BC these items became widespread in Macedonia and much of the central Balkans.

In the empire of Alexander the Great, one of the main markers of a true Greek city was the presence of an odeon for musical performances. This was the case not only for Alexandria in Egypt, but also for cities as distant as Ai-Khanoum in modern-day Afghanistan.

war.text: In 480 BC a Greek force of about 7,000 men, including an estimated 300 Spartans, marched north under Leonidas to block the pass of Thermopylae against the Persian army of Xerxes. Ancient authors vastly inflated the Persian numbers, with estimates in the millions. After three days of direct battle, the Greek rear-guard was annihilated: Leonidas was shot down by Persian archers, the Greeks fought on with swords, hands and teeth, and the Persians rained arrows on the last of them until every Greek was dead. Herodotus puts Persian dead at up to 20,000, and the king later had the surrendered Theban prisoners branded with the royal mark.

The Battle of Salamis in 480 BC was arguably the largest naval battle of the ancient world. Greek city-states under Themistocles defeated the larger fleet of Xerxes in the straits between the mainland and the island of Salamis, ramming and boarding ships in cramped waters where the Persian ships fouled one another. Herodotus says the Persians suffered many more casualties than the Greeks because most of them did not know how to swim, and Xerxes watched the carnage from a throne on Mount Aigaleo. It marked a turning point in the Persian invasion.

Ancient Greek city-states fought with a new style of warfare, the hoplite phalanx: armored citizen infantrymen with spears and shields, who collided in battles the article calls short, bloody and brutal. Since the soldiers had other jobs, war was limited in distance, season and scale, and neither side could afford heavy casualties, so conflicts seem to have been settled by a single set-piece battle. Casualties ran from about 5% for the winning side to 15% for the losing side, and the slain often included the most prominent citizens and generals who led from the front. Victory was enforced by ransoming the dead back to the defeated.
In 146 BC Rome defeated the Achaean League at the Battle of Corinth in the Achaean War. The Romans completely destroyed the city and annexed mainland Greece, bringing Greek independence to an end.

The hoplite's key innovation seems to have been the circular shield, or aspis, about 1 m (3 ft) across and made of wood faced with bronze. It could be supported on the shoulder and allowed an army to form a shield-wall. Paired with the 2 to 3 m long spear called the doru, it gave both offensive and defensive power.

Theban forces under Epaminondas defeated the Spartans at the Battle of Leuctra in 371 BC, giving rise to a short-lived Theban hegemony. Epaminondas and Pelopidas, who commanded the Sacred Band of Thebes at Leuctra, were the generals behind the rise.

In 338 BC Philip II of Macedon defeated a Greek alliance at the Battle of Chaeronea and then formed the League of Corinth. He planned to lead it against Persia but was murdered in 336 BC. His son Alexander the Great began the campaign against Persia in 334 BC.

The Chigi vase, dated to around 650 BC, is the earliest depiction of a hoplite in full battle array. By roughly that date the so-called hoplite revolution was complete. Historians debate whether the hoplite originated in the 8th century BC with Sparta or later, towards the 7th century BC.

Xerxes prepared his invasion of Greece with feats of exceptional ambition. He had a canal dug across the isthmus of Mount Athos, where a Persian fleet had been destroyed in 492 BC, and his army crossed the Hellespont on two pontoon bridges.

The Illyrian Wars, from 229 BC to 168 BC, saw Rome overrun Illyrian settlements and suppress piracy that had made the Adriatic unsafe for Roman commerce. There were three campaigns: the first against Teuta, the second against Demetrius of Pharos and the third against Gentius, whom the Romans defeated at Scodra in 168 BC. The first campaign in 229 BC marks the first time the Roman Navy crossed the Adriatic Sea to launch an invasion. Roman sources described the Illyrians as "barbarians" or "savages", and Polybius wrote that the Romans had freed the Greeks from "the enemies of all mankind".

The hoplitodromos, or hoplite race, was introduced at the Olympic Games in 520 BC. Runners covered a single or double diaulos, roughly 400 or 800 metres, in full military armour. It was based on a war tactic of soldiers running in full armor to surprise the enemy.

In wartime, soldiers used a patchwork fabric called cento in many ways. Soldiers used it as a protective layer in the trenches and as a cap under a helmet to prevent chafing. Centones were also hung on fortifications to shield them from fire and absorb the impact of weapons.

literature.text: The two epic poems the Iliad and the Odyssey are the earliest surviving works of ancient Greek literature. Together with the Homeric Hymns and Hesiod's Theogony and Works and Days, they formed the major foundations of the Greek literary tradition.

All ancient Greek literature was to some degree oral, and the earliest literature was completely so. The Greeks created poetry before using writing for literary purposes, and poems were meant to be sung or recited, since writing was little known before the 7th century BC.

Aeschylus is the earliest Greek tragic playwright for whom any plays have survived complete. Sophocles is famous for his tragedies about Oedipus, particularly Oedipus the King and Antigone, while Euripides often pushed the boundaries of the tragic genre.
Surviving Greek literature was written in a Phoenician-derived alphabet that arose primarily in Greek Ionia. Athens had fully adopted it by the fifth century BC.

Aristophanes wrote in the genre of Old Comedy, while the later playwright Menander was an early pioneer of New Comedy. Like tragedy, comedy arose from a ritual in honor of Dionysus, but its plays were full of frank obscenity, abuse and insult. Aristophanes poked fun at everyone and every institution.

In the 3rd century BC, the encyclopedic movement at Alexandria anthologized a canon of nine melic poets. They were Alcaeus, Alcman, Anacreon, Bacchylides, Ibycus, Pindar, Sappho, Simonides, and Stesichorus.

Daphnis and Chloe by Longus is by far the most famous of the five surviving ancient Greek romance novels. It is a nostalgic tale of two young lovers growing up in an idealized pastoral setting on the Greek island of Lesbos.

The earliest extant examples of ancient Greek writing, from about 1450 BC, are in the syllabic script Linear B. From the 8th century BC the Greek alphabet became standard. Early texts were written in boustrophedon style, but left-to-right became standard in the classic period.

The poems of Sappho are said to have filled nine papyrus rolls in the Library of Alexandria, with the first book alone containing more than 1,300 lines. Today only one of her poems exists intact, and fragments from other sources would scarcely fill a chapbook.

Pausanias' Description of Greece is a travel guide describing the geography and mythic history of Greece during the second century. The book takes the form of a tour that starts in Athens and ends in Naupactus.
Greek poetry meters are based on patterns of long and short syllables, unlike English verse, which is determined by stress. Lyric poetry is characterized by a great variety of metrical forms.
The Wonders Beyond Thule by Antonius Diogenes has not survived in complete form. A very lengthy summary of it, written by Photios I of Constantinople, has survived.

science.text: Greek mathematics differed from earlier civilizations' mathematics by developing mathematics as a theoretical discipline and using deductive reasoning in proofs. Treatises of deductive mathematics written in Greek began circulating around the mid-fifth century BC.

Aristarchus of Samos, in the 3rd century BCE, was the first and only premodern figure to propose a truly heliocentric model of the Solar System. He placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the universe, earning the nickname the "Ancient Copernicus".

Greek athletics became a scientific and philosophical field of study. By the fourth century BCE, sports were so competitive that specialized coaches developed for each sport, and a new four-day training cycle called the tetras was created.

Philolaus, in the 5th century BC, proposed a Pythagorean astronomical system with an unseen "Central Fire" around which all other bodies of the cosmos revolved. This fire was not the Sun. Heraclides Ponticus later posited a geo-heliocentric system in which the Sun rotated around the Earth but all other bodies rotated around the Sun.

The Greek word mathēmatikē comes from máthēma, meaning 'lesson'. Around the time of Archytas and Plato, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and harmonics were listed together as special branches of learning. They would later become the medieval quadrivium.

Hippocrates (460 BC - 377 BC), known as the "father of medicine", based his nutritional advice on the four humors in the body. Galen later admired his work and believed Hippocrates had stated all that needed to be known about nutrition.

Apollonius of Perga responded to problems in earlier astronomical theories, especially that of Eudoxus, by producing the theory of eccentrics and epicycles. Hipparchus elaborated on it in the second century BC, and Ptolemy in the 2nd century AD. The Antikythera mechanism also appears to presuppose eccentrics and epicycles in its calculations.

The theory of conic sections may be the most characteristic product of Greek mathematics. It was largely developed in the Hellenistic period, primarily by Apollonius (262-190 BC), whose methods used neither algebra nor trigonometry. Trigonometry appeared around the time of Hipparchus (190-120 BC).

Greek trainers recognized around the fifth century BCE that meat was key in building muscle. Most people ate meat only at religious festivals, but wealthy admirers' gifts let athletes afford it regularly, and Greek athletes' diets began to change.

Anaxagoras (500 BC - 428 BC) suggested that the foods we eat contain fragments needed for growth in the body. His belief was that "everything is in everything, at all times", so hair, nails and flesh were generated from foods containing those same substances.

politics.text: Ancient Greece was a loose collection of culturally related city-states and regions. Before the Roman period, most of it was officially unified only once, from 338 to 323 BC, under the Kingdom of Macedon.
The Achaean league outlasted both the Aetolian league and Macedon, but it was also soon defeated and absorbed by the Romans in 146 BC. That defeat brought Greek independence to an end.

In 330 AD the city of Byzantium, adopted by Emperor Constantine the Great as Nova Roma and capital of the Roman Empire, was renamed Constantinople. After the death of Theodosius I in 395 AD, the Roman Empire split into Western and Eastern halves.

Under Philip II (359–336 BC), Macedonia subdued mainland Greece through conquest and diplomacy. With a reformed army of phalanxes wielding the sarissa pike, he defeated the old powers of Athens and Thebes at the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BC.

Herodotus relates that Alexander I of Macedon took part in the Olympic Games in 504 or 500 BC, and other participants contested it because he was not Greek. The Hellanodikai examined his Argead claim and confirmed that the Macedonian kings were Greeks.

Artaxerxes II subsidized Sparta's enemies, including the Athenians, Thebans and Corinthians, to keep the Spartans busy in Greece, which helped spark the Corinthian War. In 387 BC he betrayed his allies the Spartans and came to an arrangement with Sparta, and in the Treaty of Antalcidas he forced them to come to terms. The treaty restored Persian control of the Greek cities of Ionia and Aeolis and gave Sparta dominance on the Greek mainland.

After Perseus lost the Third Macedonian War, the Romans abolished the Macedonian monarchy and installed four allied republics, with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. They banned marriages between the republics' inhabitants and temporarily prohibited gold and silver mining.

Antigonus II Gonatas knew the Greeks loved freedom and autonomy, so he granted a semblance of it, as far as it did not clash with his own power, and avoided the odium of direct rule by controlling them through intermediaries. Polybius says of him, "No man ever set up more absolute rulers in Greece than Antigonus." The tyrants he installed or maintained included Cleon of Sicyon and Aristotimus of Elis, who was assassinated in 272 BC. Others met the same end: Aristodemus the Good of Megalopolis was assassinated in 252 BC and Aristomachus of Argos in 240 BC.

In the winter of 279 BC, a great horde of Gauls under Brennus descended on Macedonia from the north, crushed Ptolemy's army and killed him in battle, starting two years of complete anarchy. After plundering Macedonia, the Gauls moved south and invaded further regions of Greece. In 278 BC a Greek army with a large Aetolian contingent checked the Gauls at Thermopylae and Delphi, inflicting heavy casualties and forcing them to retreat.

Greek support for Mark Antony proved ruinous. After the Second Triumvirate won the Battle of Philippi in 42 BC, Antony took the east, and Greece was physically and economically devastated by his financial demands. Augustus organised grain supplies and created the province of Achaea in 27 BC.

After the death of king Archelaus, Macedon endured a six-year interregnum from 399 to 393 BCE. Orestes, Aeropus II, Amyntas II and Pausanias fought each other over the throne. The article says the death of a king almost invariably triggered dynastic disputes, often a war of succession between members of the Argead family, leading to political and economic instability.

A man named Andriscus, claiming Antigonid descent, was pronounced king of Macedonia and defeated the Roman praetor Publius Juventius Thalna in the Fourth Macedonian War. In 148 BC Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus defeated him at the second Battle of Pydna and occupied the kingdom.

philosophy.text: Western philosophy originated in Ancient Greece in the 6th century BCE with the pre-Socratic philosophers, such as Thales of Miletus (c. 626 – c. 545 BCE). They tried to give rational explanations of the cosmos as a whole.

Socrates (469–399 BCE), Plato (427–347 BCE) and Aristotle (384–322 BCE) shaped the philosophy that followed the pre-Socratics. They widened its range to questions such as how people should act, how to arrive at knowledge, and what the nature of reality and mind is.
Hellenistic philosophy runs from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BC to the Battle of Actium in 31 BC. Its dominant schools were the Stoics, the Epicureans and the Skeptics.

According to A. C. Grayling, the greater insecurity and loss of autonomy of the Hellenistic era drove some people to use philosophy to seek inner security from the external world. Epicurus captured this idea when he claimed that "empty are the words of that philosopher who offers therapy for no human suffering".

Greek philosophical skepticism began as a distinct movement with Pyrrho of Elis and Timon of Phlius in the 3rd century BC. Around 266 BC the Platonic Academy became the main advocate of skepticism, and Arcesilaus became its head.

The Peripatetic school carried on Aristotle's philosophy after his death, beginning with Theophrastus (371–287 BC) and Strato of Lampsacus (335–269 BC). They held that the goal of life was eudaimonia, which came from virtuous actions that kept the mean between the too much and the too little.
Plato's nephew Speusippus succeeded him as head of the Old Academy, followed by Xenocrates. Both sought to fuse Pythagorean speculations on number with Plato's theory of forms.

The Academic skeptics maintained that knowledge of things is impossible and that ideas are never true. Yet they allowed degrees of truth-likeness, and so degrees of belief, which let a person act. The most extensive ancient source on them is Cicero's Academica.

Classical thinkers were mostly based in Athens, but by the end of the Hellenistic period philosophers had relocated to Rome or Alexandria. Sulla's capture of Athens in 87 BC led to destructions and to the shipping of Aristotle's manuscripts to Rome.
In the 1st century BC, Aenesidemus broke with the Academic skeptics and adopted Pyrrhonism. He denounced the Academy as "Stoics fighting against Stoics".

In the first century BCE, the naked Indian philosopher and monk Zarmanochegas (possibly, but not necessarily, a Buddhist) met Nicholas of Damascus in Antioch and later traveled to Athens. There he burned himself to death in 19 BCE. According to Plutarch, writing near the end of the first century CE or the beginning of the second, his tomb could still be seen in Athens.

culture.text: Theatre was born in Greece, and Classical Athens was its centre. There it was institutionalised as part of a festival called the Dionysia, which honoured the god Dionysus. Tragedy, comedy and the satyr play all emerged there.
Religious festivals filled the Athenian calendar. The year in Athens included some 140 days that were religious festivals of some sort, though they varied greatly in importance.

Most ancient Greeks recognized twelve major Olympian gods and goddesses, including Zeus, Hera, Poseidon and Athena. The Greeks did not have a word for 'religion' in the modern sense. Herodotus instead spoke of the Hellenes as having common shrines of the gods and sacrifices, and the same kinds of customs.

Ancient Greek clothing was often colorful, using black, red, yellow, blue, green and purple. The elite typically wore purple as a sign of wealth, since it was the most expensive dye due to the difficulty in acquiring it.
The ancient Olympic Games were not only a sporting event. Like the other Panhellenic Games, they were a religious festival, held at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia.

Comedy first appeared in Athens in 486 BC, and tragedy in the late 6th century BC. Athens exported the Dionysia festival to its numerous colonies and allies in order to promote a common cultural identity.

In classical times, city-states held festivals and rituals throughout the year, with particular emphasis on their patron god. Athena was the patron of Athens, while Apollo held that role at Corinth. Each god was honored with stone temples, statues and sanctuaries.
The festival of Lykaia was celebrated in Arcadia in Greece and was dedicated to the pastoral god Pan. Many Greek festivals were specific only to a particular deity or city-state.

More typical Greek festivals featured a procession, large sacrifices and a feast to eat the offerings. The animals were slaughtered over the altar, their blood was collected and poured over it, and they were butchered on the spot, with the meat prepared for the feast. At large festivals the number of cattle sacrificed could run into the hundreds, and the numbers feasting on them well into the thousands. Customs also included visiting friends, wearing fancy dress and unusual behavior in the streets, sometimes risky for bystanders in various ways.

The island of Delos was sacred as the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis. As a major port and trading center, it also hosted cult centers for the Egyptian Sarapis and Isis and the Syrian Atargatis and Hadad. By the 1st century BCE it even had a Jewish Synagogue.

The Macedonians continued Archaic burial practices that had ceased in other parts of Greece after the 6th century BC. Otherwise their religious beliefs mirrored those of other Greeks, following the main deities of the Greek pantheon.

By the latter 6th century BC, Macedonian elites could acquire exotic Aegean items such as Athenian red figure pottery, perfume flasks, wine amphorae and glass. These items served as status symbols. By the 5th century BC they had become widespread in Macedonia and much of the central Balkans.
